extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; general educated readers and students of essays/philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A translation excerpt from Montaigne's Essays discussing moderation, pleasure, dining, aging, and how to live; contains prescriptive and reflective statements about conduct and the enjoyment of life. Useful for literary, philosophical, or pedagogical analysis of ethical and practical maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer assisting those in greatest need
rubrics_metrics.description: “I should rather regard them who extend their arms to me, than those who turn their backs upon me.” Prefer to give help to the meanest/most needy rather than curry favour with the powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explains this as both honourable and compassionate, giving examples and contrasts (e.g., Flaminius who aided the needy vs. Pyrrhus who truckled to the great). The criterion discourages helping only for reciprocal gain; favor the party who most needs assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mean is best / prefer moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne repeatedly endorses the maxim that 'the mean is best' and that moderate measures are the most perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He cites Stoic/Socratic temperaments and classical authorities to show that balance between extremes (neither wholly contemplative nor wholly sensual) is virtuous. Greatness of soul is shown by governing and circumscribing oneself and preferring moderate to eminent things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eat leisurely and intermix eating with profitable conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Eating and drinking should be performed deliberately, at leisure, and intermingled with profitable conversation; the ancients had more reason to set apart many hours for eating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises long, deliberate meals for digestion and social pleasure, and criticizes hasty modern habits. He recommends good company and suitable discourse during meals and warns against being a talker on a full stomach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value company at table — who you eat with matters
rubrics_metrics.description: One is 'not so much to regard what he eats, as with whom'—the sociability of the meal is a principal part of its pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He commends Chilo's practice of asking who will be present before attending a feast. The art of dining well includes agreeable conversation, graceful presence, neatness, and appropriate company (Varro's list). Avoid musical distractions when it indicates lack of good discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance is the seasoning of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Intemperance is the pest of pleasure; temperance is not its scourge but rather its seasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that temperance allows one to taste pleasures fully and that extreme abstinence or excess both spoil the good. He uses classical examples (Euxodus) to show temperance makes pleasures charming and sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savor present pleasures deliberately (ruminate on them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'pass away' good time; 'I taste it over again and adhere to it' — one should study, taste, and ruminate upon present content to amplify and extend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical techniques: attend mindfully to contentment, associate the soul to bodily pleasure (without losing oneself), deliberately recall comparisons with less fortunate conditions, and even interrupt sleep to better relish it. This is prescribed as a way to deepen life's enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate bodily and intellectual pleasures; reject strict ascetic separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy that despises bodily pleasures is childish; one should not divorce the divine/intellectual from the earthly/carnal — reconcile mind and body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne critiques extremes (Aristippus privileging body; Zeno privileging soul) and praises a Socratic mean that values both. He argues it is unjust to refuse or disfigure nature's gifts; bodily pleasures are natural and worthy when governed by reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortitude must oppose both pain and immoderate pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be equally the office of fortitude to fight against pain and against the immoderate and charming blandishments of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Plato, Montaigne frames moral strength as resisting both undue suffering and seductive excess. Pleasure and pain are twin fountains to be drawn from as needed; prudence and fortitude regulate their use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish adherence to enforced or superstitious rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit to enforced, superstitious, or escalating rules (e.g., accreting layers of clothing or ritualized regimens) because they lead to endless additions and loss of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns how small accommodations (cap, quilted hat, hare's skin) escalate into burdensome habits. He recommends avoiding such escalations and the rigid invariable forms (e.g., in fasting) that harden the body and limit liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make fasting or rigid regimens universal — vary according to needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid invariable fasting or fixed forms; if one hardens oneself into a regimen, one loses liberty and may suffer by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne describes using fasting sometimes to sharpen appetite or preserve vigor, but cautions against making one form always serve; adaptation and moderation are healthier than dogmatic persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept natural aging and death as just and (relatively) pleasant
rubrics_metrics.description: Meditate on death and accept aging as natural; death by old age is easiest and a consolation because it is just and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He comforts himself by noting gradual decay (teeth falling, senses dimming) and cites authorities (Plato, Cicero) who contrast violent death with mature natural death. This acceptance reduces fear and accords with living according to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure, relaxation, and play are compatible with greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Relaxation, facility, and playing (songs, sports, dancing) wonderfully honour and best become a strong and generous soul; great men may and should partake in leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives examples (Epaminondas, Scipio, Socrates) who mixed high activity with childlike or social play. He argues that such relaxation strengthens the mind and is an appropriate part of a well-lived life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to common usage in minor manners
rubrics_metrics.description: For minor customs (e.g., diluting wine), the most usual and common method of living is the most becoming; 'Public usage gives the law in these things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes variations (mixing wine with water) and suggests decency often follows public custom; do not make eccentricity in trivial matters a point of pride.
